figures.caption: FIG. 7. (a) The exciton transfer rate, RET, computed using Eq. (22) exhibits a pronounced turnover as a function of the average fraction of CT basis configurations, f̄CT. (b) The bath spectral density, S(f̄CT), increases with CT character because of enhanced system–environment coupling. (c) The spatial overlap factor, P (f̄CT), decreases as disorder increases, indicating stronger exciton localization. (d) The inverse participation factor, 1/Neff , likewise indicates reduced exciton delocalization with increasing CT character. The overall transfer rate results from the competition among these effects, showing that intermediate FE–CT hybridization maximizes the exciton transfer rate.

FIG. 2. Exciton quenching dynamics are investigated by comparing transient absorption measurements on Y6 films (a) without and (b) with the copper(I) thiocyanate hole-transport layer (HTL). (c) Photoexcitation generates excitons that undergo transport and subsequent interfacial hole transfer to the HTL on a picosecond timescale, followed by charge recombination and recovery of the ground state on nanosecond timescales.

FIG. 5. (a) Transient absorption spectra of Y6 films at selected pump–probe delay times. The spectra exhibit a negative signal at shorter wavelengths, attributed primarily to ground-state bleach, and a photoinduced absorption feature at longer wavelengths. A minimum in the signal magnitude near 800 nm arises from partial cancellation between these contributions. (b) Difference signal Q(λ, τ) obtained from normalized transient absorption measurements acquired with and without the CuSCN hole-transport layer, highlighting the contribution from interfacial charge separation.
